newsitem.title: HONG KONG: World cobalt supply seen healthy despite Zaire.
newsitem.headline: World cobalt supply seen healthy despite Zaire.

text.p: The world's cobalt supplies will remain healthy, regardless of whether Zaire develops its cobalt projects, Peter Searle, head of U.K.-based Resource Strategies said at a conference on Thursday.

"There should be more than enough for the next three or four years from existing and committed supply sources if Gecamines continues production," Searle said in a presentation to cobalt industry representatives.
"If it does not, the market will move much closer to balance once again."
Fresh instability in Zaire had given new momentum to planned projects outside of Africa, particularly the lateritic nickel deposits in Australia, he said.
Searle was speaking at a conference organised by the Cobalt Development Institute in Hong Kong.
He estimated that in 1996 around 12,000 tonnes of low grade material was processed -- 9,000 tonnes from primary sources and around 3,000 tonnes from scrap and residue.
He said there was a resistance point of around US$15 per pound as this price was required to ensure a supply of cobalt through the processing of intermediate and low grade material.
But Searle estimated that if all possible projects materialised, there could be a surplus of cobalt shortly after 2000.

"I think a price of $6 per pound or even lower is possible but at this price risk may deter some future projects. The probability is that our forecast oversupply will not occur in its entirety," he said, noting that prices were likely to stay well above $6 per pound.
On Wednesday, cobalt was quoted at $24.25/25.25 per pound for cathodes and $21.75/22.75 per pound for ingots.

Zaire projects had attracted substantial investment interest, Searle said, adding that beneath political turmoil lay vast tailing deposits that could be developed into very low cost copper and cobalt operations.
"We estimate that over US$200 million of equity has so far been raised for their development and several feasibility studies for projects are underway," he said.
Worldwide cobalt consumption in 1996 was 23,500 tonnes, Searle estimated.
Searle said he believed supply fell slightly in 1995 and that in 1996 both Western production and supply were similar to 1990 levels when supply reached an all-time high.
"These two factors, I believe, explain the recent price trends," he said.
